title: A Real Village Frozen in the 1600s
summary: A walk through Culross, Fife: a real 17th-century village where seven real stops — Culross Palace, the Townhouse, the Mercat Cross, the Biscuit Cafe, Tanhouse Brae, and the old Boat House — sit almost untouched by the last 400 years. Also, unmissably, Outlander's Cranesmuir.

title: The Boy Who Invented the Propeller
summary: A real, still-working fishing harbour beneath the ruins of Dunbar Castle, where creel boats land prawns, lobster and crab most days of the week. Robert Wilson, born in a cottage here in 1803, built a working screw propeller model in 1827 and tested it on the Forth — the Royal Navy turned him down, and history mostly forgot him too. Today there's a monument on the quay, a seasonal seafood shack called Nauti, and a stretch of harbour wall covered in decades of hand-painted boat name plaques.

title: The World's Smallest Lighthouse
summary: Tucked under the shadow of the Forth Bridge sits a tiny working light tower — usually dated to 1817, dark for decades, and lit again since 2010. It's a genuine curiosity most people driving straight past never notice.

title: The Park a Billionaire Gave Away
summary: As a boy, Andrew Carnegie was banned from the private grounds of Pittencrieff Estate. Decades later, having become one of the richest men in the world, he bought the entire estate — and gave it to the town of Dunfermline. Today it's 76 acres of parkland, ruins, and free-roaming peacocks, still free to everyone.

title: The Fort That Never Fired a Shot
summary: A listed red-sandstone gun battery on Lamer Island, Dunbar Harbour, with sixteen gun embrasures. Listed as built in 1781, though the site's own board gives the Napoleonic period, and said never to have fired in anger.

title: Privately Owned Now
summary: A walk to Barns Ness Lighthouse, East Lothian: a 37m Stevenson tower built in 1899–1901, decommissioned in 2005, then sold in 2007 to the cement company next door — privately owned, not government property. One of the best fossil coastlines in east-central Scotland sits right at its feet.

title: The Harbour Village Painted in Colour
summary: A working East Neuk fishing harbour, boats still coming in daily, wrapped around a decades-old arts festival and murals of puffins and seals. Real fishing village, real art trail, one of Fife's most photographed corners.

title: Limekilns, Fife | A Path Made of Memories
summary: A port given to Dunfermline Abbey by David II in 1362, now a harbour of moored boats, and Beacon Way, a path of engraved memorial stones on the pier that ends on a question.

title: The Fishwives' Harbour | Newhaven, Edinburgh
summary: A former fishing harbour inside Edinburgh, reached by tram: the 1896 Fishmarket, two lighthouses, and the fishwives photographed by Hill and Adamson in the 1840s.
